title: Jihad: The Islamic Doctrine of Permanent War
byline: by Suhas Majumdar · Voice of India · 1994 · enlarged from a Bengali monograph, with a foreword by Sita Ram Goel
lede: Majumdar, a mathematician by training, sets out to describe jihad as Islam's own sources define it. He works through the Quran (in Pickthall's translation), the Hadis collections, the Prophet's practice (the Sunnah) and the Hanafi law code Hidayah. His conclusion is that jihad means aggressive war to spread Islam, and he says the modern defensive readings do not fit the texts. He also argues that Hindus who translate jihad as dharmayuddha, a war fought by rules of restraint, misunderstand it.

note: This is a hostile reading of Islamic doctrine. Muslim scholars, and many historians, read the same verses differently. They stress context, the rules of war in Islamic law, and jihad as inner striving. This page sets out Majumdar's argument and sources, attributed to him, and does not settle how jihad should be understood.

items: “Fight… against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities.” Majumdar argues that read with Surah 9 it does not limit jihad to self-defence. Many Muslim commentators disagree.

The Afghan historian Ahmad Yadgar and Badauni say the boy Akbar struck the captive Hemu and took the title ghazi. Abul Fazl's account says he refused. Majumdar reads the court historians' version as Akbar distancing himself from jihad.
